title: Accent Change May Be Sign of a Good Ear — Study
paragraphs: Have you ever noticed that some people's accents change when they move to a new place, while others keep the same accent for their whole lives? Research suggests that the ability to copy an accent may be connected to having a good ear.

In a study published in the journal Open Mind, researchers at the University of Connecticut in the US looked at why some people are better at imitating accents than others. The study was led by Emily Myers. It included 92 adults whose first language was English. Some of them were actors or drama students, and almost half were musicians.

The participants listened to short phrases spoken in three different accents: from Yorkshire in England, from Edinburgh in Scotland, and from the Eastern Cape in South Africa. They then tried to copy each accent. More than 1,000 people online listened to the recordings and rated how similar each attempt was to the real accent.

The participants also took several tests. One test measured how well they could hear differences in music, such as in melody and rhythm. Another measured how quickly they could move their mouths to say syllables. They also answered questions about their personalities.

The researchers found that people who were better at hearing differences in music were better at copying accents. People who could say syllables more quickly also did better. In addition, people who were more open to new experiences tended to be better at imitating accents.
Interestingly, people's feelings about the speakers also mattered. When participants thought a speaker was competent, they copied that speaker's accent better.
Earlier research in Austria found a similar result. People who were good at singing were also better at faking a French accent.
However, the researchers say that their study does not prove that these skills cause better imitation. More research is needed.
